cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: Basics and rationale
cards.front: What are the ACTIONES ADIECTITIAE QUALITATIS?
cards.back:
'Additional' actions extending a creditor's contractual claim against a (typically asset-less) debtor to the principal behind him, who can be expected to pay.
• Mostly against the DOMINUS / PATER FAMILIAS for debts of persons in power.
• DE PECULIO, DE IN REM VERSO, QUOD IUSSU: debtor must be in the principal's power.
• EXERCITORIA, INSTITORIA: debtor may be in nobody's power or another's.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: Basics and rationale
cards.front: Example 74 (livestock trader Clemens): Ago buys a pig and Bellona a goose on credit — what is Clemens' problem?
cards.back:
Ago is a son in power, Bellona is Dexter's slave: neither can actually pay Clemens.
• Ago can be sued, but owns nothing — the judgment cannot be enforced.
• Bellona owns nothing and, as a slave, cannot even be sued.
• Solution: extend the claim to the power-holder, e.g. Dexter's letter = IUSSUM → ACTIO QUOD IUSSU.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: Basics and rationale
cards.front: Which two rationales justify holding a principal liable ADIECTITIAE QUALITATIS?
cards.back:
Benefit and trust.
• Benefit: the principal profits from business run by his 'manager', so he answers for its debts.
• Trust: a creditor who reasonably relied on the principal's wealth may reach it.
• Example 74 variant: Clemens relied on Dexter's IUSSUM → ACTIO QUOD IUSSU.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: Basics and rationale
cards.front: Paulus D 14.1.5.1: how is liability ADIECTITIAE QUALITATIS built into the formula?
cards.back:
Not as an independent claim: the contractual claim is extended to a further debtor — NON TRANSFERTUR ACTIO, SED ADICITUR.
• Example 74: ACTIO VENDITI with a QUOD IUSSU clause added to its formula.
• Modern contrast: direct agency makes the principal the contracting party from the outset.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: Basics and rationale
cards.front: Are contractual debts of slaves and children in power legally relevant at all?
cards.back:
Yes: they bind as natural obligations (OBLIGATIONES NATURALES) — not enforceable, but validly performable.
• Sons in power incur enforceable obligations (Gaius D 44.7.39), but execution fails: no property.
• Daughters in power, UXORES IN MANU, slaves: no enforceable obligations (Gai Inst 3.104).

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: Basics and rationale
cards.front: Property link: why can a slave or son in power not pay his own debts, and what does a PECULIUM change?
cards.back:
Persons in power own nothing: whatever they acquire belongs to the DOMINUS / PATER FAMILIAS.
• PECULIUM = assets the DOMINUS leaves to the dependant's independent management — legally still the DOMINUS'.
• Through it the dependant acquires possession and ownership for him, even without his knowledge.
• The price: the DOMINUS becomes liable for the dependant's debts by ACTIO DE PECULIO.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: ACTIO DE PECULIO
cards.front: When does liability by ACTIO DE PECULIO arise, and which debts does it cover?
cards.back:
When a power-holder grants a PECULIUM: he becomes liable for the dependant's contractual debts.
• Every contractual obligation — not only those linked to the grantor's economic aims.
• Grantor cannot restrict it: Gaius D 15.1.29.1 (Case 243/1), Paulus D 15.1.47 pr (Case 243/2).
• Contrast: limits on an INSTITOR's PRAEPOSITIO are valid.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: ACTIO DE PECULIO
cards.front: ACTIO DE PECULIO: is the DOMINUS liable PRO VIRIBUS or CUM VIRIBUS?
cards.back:
PRO VIRIBUS: capped at the PECULIUM's value, but the creditor can reach all the DOMINUS' assets.
• CUM VIRIBUS would mean liability limited to particular assets.
• Cap = value of the PECULIUM at the time of judgment.
• The dependant's own liability is unlimited (relevant on release, Ulpian D 15.1.44).

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: ACTIO DE PECULIO
cards.front: How is the PECULIUM valued for the ACTIO DE PECULIO?
cards.back:
At judgment: its assets, minus the DOMINUS' claims against it, plus the dependant's claims against the DOMINUS.
• Deduction: Tubero (Celsus) in Ulpian D 15.1.5.4 (Case 241/1).
• Effect: the grantor ranks before all other creditors.
• But his own debts to the PECULIUM count as its assets.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: ACTIO DE PECULIO
cards.front: Example 75: Hera lent 1,000 to slave Anicius' PECULIUM and owes him 250; Anicius owes Pomona 700; the PECULIUM holds 1,400. What does Pomona get?
cards.back:
650 from Hera, by ACTIO VENDITI as ACTIO DE PECULIO.
• 1,400 − 1,000 (Hera's claim) + 250 (Hera's debt) = 650.
• The remaining 50 cannot be recovered this way.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: ACTIO DE PECULIO
cards.front: Ulpian D 15.1.21 pr (Case 242): may the DOMINUS shrink the PECULIUM to escape its creditors?
cards.back:
He may withdraw or reshape it at any time, but dolose changes do not reduce his ACTIO DE PECULIO liability.
• Withdrawal → DOLUS presumed; also a slave deliberately muddling the PECULIUM.
• Strict rule: once a suit is foreseeable, every change counts as dolose.
• Not dolose: paying a creditor from the PECULIUM — lowers the cap legitimately.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: ACTIO DE PECULIO
cards.front: Example 76: Galenus' PECULIUM (900) owes Omphale 800 and Menander 300; Omphale wins judgment first. Result?
cards.back:
Omphale recovers 800 in full; Menander, suing later, gets only 100.
• Creditors are paid in the order they enforce, until the cap is used up.
• No pro-rata distribution as in insolvency.
• Exception MERX PECULIARIS → ACTIO TRIBUTORIA (not ADIECTITIAE QUALITATIS).

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: DE IN REM VERSO and QUOD IUSSU
cards.front: What is the ACTIO DE IN REM VERSO, and when is it typically invoked?
cards.back:
Liability of the DOMINUS insofar as he is enriched (VERSIO) through the business of a person in his power.
• Stands beside DE PECULIO in the same part of the formula.
• Used where there is no PECULIUM or the claim exceeds it (Servius in Alfenus D 15.3.16, Case 245).

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: DE IN REM VERSO and QUOD IUSSU
cards.front: Which three kinds of benefit to the DOMINUS count as VERSIO?
cards.back:
Discharge of his debt, his necessary expenses, absorption into his regular capital.
• Ex 77: slave Maevius borrows from Felix and pays Scipio's 300 rent.
• Ex 78: son Victor buys bread and wine on credit for Scipio's unfed slaves.
• Ex 79: Maevius buys seed and sows a field Scipio runs himself.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: DE IN REM VERSO and QUOD IUSSU
cards.front: What is the DOMINUS' 'regular capital', and why does it matter for VERSIO?
cards.back:
Assets he manages directly, not through dependants deciding independently; what is absorbed into it enriches him.
• Neratius (Paulus D 15.3.19 pr): son's toga, unknowingly used for his funeral → IN REM PATRIS VERSUM.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: DE IN REM VERSO and QUOD IUSSU
cards.front: ACTIO DE IN REM VERSO vs ACTIO QUOD IUSSU — how much does the creditor recover?
cards.back:
DE IN REM VERSO: at most the enrichment, and never more than the agreed price; QUOD IUSSU: the full contractual claim.
• Cap of the VERSIO: Gaius D 15.3.12 (Case 244).
• No actual VERSIO, no claim — even if pretended (Ulpian D 15.3.3.9, Case 247).

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: DE IN REM VERSO and QUOD IUSSU
cards.front: Julian in Africanus D 15.3.17 pr (Case 248): a slave borrows for his DOMINUS but loses the money without fault before using it. VERSIO?
cards.back:
Yes, if he genuinely meant to use it for the DOMINUS: VERSIO occurs already with the DATIO to the slave.
• Probably beyond the prevailing view.
• Parallel to UTILITER COEPTUM in NEGOTIORUM GESTIO: usefulness judged ex ante.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: DE IN REM VERSO and QUOD IUSSU
cards.front: What are the requirements of liability by ACTIO QUOD IUSSU?
cards.back:
The DOMINUS authorised the dependant to contract (IUSSUM), the third party learned of it and contracted relying on it.
• Clear application of the reliance principle (Gai Inst 4.70).
• Form free; one deal or a whole class of contracts (Ulpian D 15.4.1.1, Case 249).
• Later approval (RATIHABITIO) suffices too (Ulpian D 15.4.1.6, Case 250).

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: DE IN REM VERSO and QUOD IUSSU
cards.front: Property link: IUSSUM to contract vs IUSSUM to acquire ownership through a dependant — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Acquisition IUSSUM mainly expresses the DOMINUS' ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI; third-party reliance plays no role.
• Contracting IUSSUM matters because the third party relies on it.
• Property law: without IUSSUM or PECULIUM no acquisition, unless approved later (RATIHABITIO).

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: EXERCITORIA and INSTITORIA
cards.front: ACTIO EXERCITORIA — who is liable, and for what?
cards.back:
The ship operator (EXERCITOR) who made known he appointed a captain (MAGISTER NAVIS) answers for the captain's business obligations.
• Unqualified PRAEPOSITIO: carriage, supplies, repairs, wages (Ulpian D 14.1.1.7, Case 252).
• Narrowed by declaration: freight-only captain charters whole ship → no liability (D 14.1.1.12, Case 253).
• Captain may be in the operator's power, another's, or nobody's.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: EXERCITORIA and INSTITORIA
cards.front: ACTIO INSTITORIA — who is liable, and what is the PRAEPOSITIO?
cards.back:
A business owner who made known he appointed a manager (INSTITOR) answers for obligations causally connected with the business.
• PRAEPOSITIO = externally recognisable appointment as manager.
• Ordinary course includes a business loan (Ulpian D 14.3.5.13, Case 257).
• Explicitly forbidden borrowing → no ACTIO INSTITORIA for the loan.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: EXERCITORIA and INSTITORIA
cards.front: Ulpian D 14.3.5.10 (Case 259): a laundry owner leaving on a journey puts an assistant in charge. Liability ADIECTITIAE QUALITATIS?
cards.back:
Only if the assistant was authorised to deal with third parties (INSTITOR), not for mere internal administration (PROCURATOR).
• INSTITOR = external business; PROCURATOR = internal administration.
• Recent scholarship: probably one of his assistants (DISCIPULUS), not an outsider.

cards.topic: Ch. XI — Actiones adiectitiae qualitatis: EXERCITORIA and INSTITORIA
cards.front: PROCURATOR vs INSTITOR — and what did Papinian's ACTIO QUASI INSTITORIA add?
cards.back:
PROCURATOR administers internally, INSTITOR deals externally; Papinian extended institorial liability to procurators.
• PROCURATOR PRAEPOSITUS for loans → DOMINUS liable alongside him (Papinian D 14.3.19 pr, Case 260).
• Even without PRAEPOSITIO: buyer knew of and relied on the mandate (D 19.1.13.25, Case 261).
• Most important step toward direct agency; cf § 1029 ABGB apparent authority.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Concept and another's affairs
cards.front: What is NEGOTIORUM GESTIO?
cards.back:
Deliberately taking care of another's affairs without being bound or authorised by mandate or other contract.
• Intervener = NEGOTIORUM GESTOR; principal = DOMINUS NEGOTII.
• Origin AMICITIA: defending an ABSENS INDEFENSUS in court to avert MISSIO IN BONA.
• A quasi-contract: duties arise from a contract-like factual situation.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Concept and another's affairs
cards.front: ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM DIRECTA vs CONTRARIA?
cards.back:
Both BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA: DIRECTA = principal against gestor; CONTRARIA = gestor against principal.
• DIRECTA: for what was obtained and, where relevant, damages.
• CONTRARIA: for certain expenses and losses.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Concept and another's affairs
cards.front: MANDATUM vs NEGOTIORUM GESTIO — common ground and difference?
cards.back:
Both: (free) management of another's affairs; only mandate rests on an agreement grounding rights and duties.
• NEGOTIORUM GESTIO is therefore classed as a quasi-contract.
• In both, mixed interests suffice.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Concept and another's affairs
cards.front: When is an affair 'another's' (NEGOTIUM ALIENUM), and which intent must the gestor have?
cards.back:
It must fall within or directly benefit the principal's sphere; gestor acts with ANIMUS REM ALTERI GERENDI.
• Nursing another's sick slave (C 2.18(19).10, Case 220).
• Shoring up another's collapsing house (Ulpian D 3.5.9(10).1, Case 219).
• Paying another's debts (Labeo D 3.5.42(43), Case 222/1); court representation.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Concept and another's affairs
cards.front: Example 80: co-owner Aron repairs the common roof for 10,000 without asking co-owner Iokaste. Claim?
cards.back:
Yes: as NEGOTIORUM GESTOR he can claim half (5,000) from Iokaste.
• The necessary repair benefits him, but also serves her — mixed interest suffices.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Concept and another's affairs
cards.front: Do services rendered out of family duty (PIETAS) found a gestor's claim?
cards.back:
No: support from legal duty or PIETAS is not NEGOTIUM ALIENUM — no reimbursement.
• Parents (Case 225), stepparents (Case 226), uncle for niece (Modestinus D 3.5.26(27).1, Case 224).
• Expecting reimbursement (ANIMUS RECIPIENDI) → ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA.
• Donation or gestio? Circumstances decide (Celsus D 24.1.47, Case 227).

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Usefulness and expenses
cards.front: Usefulness (NEGOTIUM UTILITER GESTUM): which two pairs of criteria exist, and which does Roman law apply?
cards.back:
Objective vs subjective, ex ante vs ex post; Roman law: subjective usefulness, judged ex ante (UTILITER COEPTUM).
• Subjective: how this principal himself would have acted — individualistic.
• Ex ante: judged when the gestor starts, not by success.
• Necessitous intervention is usually in the principal's interest.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Usefulness and expenses
cards.front: Ulpian (Labeo, Proculus, Celsus) D 3.5.9(10).1 (Case 219): A props up B's house, which burns anyway; A nurses B's slave, who dies. Claim?
cards.back:
Yes: expenses recoverable — usefulness at the start counts, not success (Labeo; Julian).
• Proculus: house that B had abandoned (derelinquished) → no claim, it would burden B.
• Celsus: there the gestio was not subjectively useful.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Usefulness and expenses
cards.front: Which expenses can a NEGOTIORUM GESTOR recover?
cards.back:
Necessary (IMPENSAE NECESSARIAE) and, as a rule, useful ones (IMPENSAE UTILES); never luxury (IMPENSAE VOLUPTATIS CAUSA).
• Necessary: avert destruction or deterioration, e.g. putting out a fire.
• Useful: raise the asset's value.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Usefulness and expenses
cards.front: Modestinus D 3.5.26(27) pr (Case 221): adult A builds on land co-owned with his minor brother B; after division A wants the added value. Claim?
cards.back:
No reimbursement for expenses made VOLUPTATIS CAUSA rather than RE URGENTE.
• E contrario: necessary and useful expenses reimbursable.
• Or RE URGENTE limits A to necessary expenses, protecting the minor co-owner.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Gestor's liability and PROHIBENTE DOMINO
cards.front: What is the NEGOTIORUM GESTOR's standard of liability, and when is it lowered or raised?
cards.back:
In principle OMNIS CULPA — DOLUS and CULPA (Pomponius D 3.5.10(11), Case 217).
• Lowered: necessitous intervention → only DOLUS.
• Raised: deals the principal does not usually make → even chance losses.
• Reason: ambivalence of friendly help vs interference.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Gestor's liability and PROHIBENTE DOMINO
cards.front: Ulpian (Labeo) D 3.5.3.9 (Case 218): A steps in to save friend B from imminent bankruptcy and negligently causes a loss. Liable?
cards.back:
No: in necessitous intervention the gestor answers only for DOLUS — justified by AEQUITAS.
• Cf § 680 BGB: intent and gross negligence only.

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Gestor's liability and PROHIBENTE DOMINO
cards.front: Pomponius (Proculus) D 3.5.10(11) (Case 217): while B is away, A buys untrained slaves — a deal B never makes — and B suffers loss. Liable?
cards.back:
Yes, even without fault: the gestor bears losses from unusual dealings.
• Profit from such a deal goes to the principal.
• Profit and loss together: COMPENSATIO LUCRI CUM DAMNO (cf § 1312 ABGB).

cards.topic: Ch. XII — Negotiorum gestio: Gestor's liability and PROHIBENTE DOMINO
cards.front: NEGOTIORUM GESTIO PROHIBENTE DOMINO — may the gestor claim his expenses?
cards.back:
Disputed: some grant an ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM or ACTIO UTILIS; Julian, Paulus and Pomponius deny any action.
• Against: the principal's declared will must be respected.
• For: the principal is enriched, e.g. released by the surety's payment.
• Paulus D 17.1.40 (Case 223/1); Justinian C 2.18(19).24 (Case 223/2).

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Concept and FIDEIUSSIO
cards.front: What is suretyship, and which relationships does it create?
cards.back:
A further person besides the debtor becomes personally liable with all his assets for the debtor's debt.
• Contract creditor–surety, tied to the primary debt: three-person relationship.
• Internal relationship surety–debtor: usually mandate or NEGOTIORUM GESTIO.
• Standing surety = intercession (INTERCEDERE); SC VELLEIANUM: women → EXCEPTIO SC VELLEIANI.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Concept and FIDEIUSSIO
cards.front: Suretyship vs pledge — advantages and disadvantages for the creditor?
cards.back:
Surety: execution against all his assets, but only in personam; pledge: only the thing, but with priority.
• Insolvent surety → creditor satisfied only pro rata.
• Pledgee holds a right in rem: priority even in the debtor's bankruptcy.
• Ex 81: Pelias guarantees Nike's 10,000 loan from Agamemnon.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Concept and FIDEIUSSIO
cards.front: How is a FIDEIUSSIO concluded?
cards.back:
By STIPULATIO — creditor asks, guarantor answers yes: QUOD MAEVIUS MIHI DEBET, ID FIDE TUA ESSE IUBES?
• A verbal contract; the most important classical form of suretyship.
• Forerunners SPONSIO, FIDEPROMISSIO secure only stipulated claims (others first novated).

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Concept and FIDEIUSSIO
cards.front: Classical FIDEIUSSOR: equal-ranking or subsidiary — and what did Justinian change?
cards.back:
Classical: equal-ranking alternative debtor; Justinian: subsidiary through the BENEFICIUM EXCUSSIONIS.
• Classical creditor chooses; procedural consumption bars suing the other afterwards.
• BENEFICIUM EXCUSSIONIS: creditor must first go to the primary obligor.
• Modern: subsidiarity and accessoriness; but guarantor-and-payer, § 1357 ABGB.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Accessoriness and objections
cards.front: What does accessoriness of the FIDEIUSSOR's obligation mean?
cards.back:
Existence, continuance and amount of his debt depend on the principal debt — he promises QUOD MAEVIUS DEBET.
• SPONSIO / FIDEPROMISSIO instead follow the debtor's original verbal promise.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Accessoriness and objections
cards.front: Paulus D 46.1.56.2 (Case 51 a): G lends D a third party's coins; B guarantees repayment by FIDEIUSSIO. Is B bound?
cards.back:
At delivery no: ownership did not pass, so no MUTUUM arose. Once D spends the coins, B is liable (CONDICTIO).
• Spending makes D owner and obliges him to repay.
• B guarantees every legal ground arising from the money transfer.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Accessoriness and objections
cards.front: Property link: NUMMOS CONSUMERE — why does spending another's coins matter for loans and suretyship?
cards.back:
Spending or mixing the coins makes the recipient owner originally, though no valid transfer occurred.
• Before spending: the owner can still vindicate the coins (REI VINDICATIO).
• After: only a CONDICTIO for repayment — which a FIDEIUSSOR can secure (Case 51 a).
• Thief who mixes coins: CONDICTIO FURTIVA.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Accessoriness and objections
cards.front: Which of the debtor's defences may the guarantor raise, and which not?
cards.back:
Defences concerning the debt itself — even against the debtor's will; not strictly personal ones.
• Yes: EXCEPTIO DOLI, QUOD METUS CAUSA, REI IUDICATAE, PACTI DE NON PETENDO, SC MACEDONIANI.
• No: BENEFICIUM COMPETENTIAE (ID QUOD FACERE POTEST), e.g. husband restoring the DOS.
• Marcian D 44.1.19 (Case 51 b); Paulus D 44.1.7.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Accessoriness and objections
cards.front: Can a natural obligation be secured by FIDEIUSSIO — a slave's loan, or a loan against the SC MACEDONIANUM?
cards.back:
Yes: the creditor may sue the surety although the slave's debt is unenforceable.
• SC MACEDONIANUM loan: also imperfect, but the EXCEPTIO is factual — the guarantor can raise it.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Recourse
cards.front: What is the guarantor's recourse, and which action does he use?
cards.back:
His right to reimbursement from the person whose debt it materially is; the action follows the internal relationship.
• Mandate → ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA.
• NEGOTIORUM GESTIO → ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA.
• Or assignment of the creditor's claim (BENEFICIUM CEDENDARUM ACTIONUM).

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Recourse
cards.front: When is the surety–debtor relationship a mandate, and what follows from it?
cards.back:
When he stands surety at the debtor's request or apparent approval, e.g. in his presence (Ulpian D 17.1.6.2).
• His payment = expense of the mandate → ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA.
• Mutual duties: e.g. notify the other before paying, to avoid double payment.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Recourse
cards.front: Ulpian D 17.1.29.3 (Case 177): surety G pays creditor C without telling mandator D; D then pays C again. G's recourse?
cards.back:
No ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA: failing to inform comes very close to DOLUS (CULPA LATA).
• G may demand that D cede his CONDICTIO INDEBITI against C.
• So G bears the risk of C's insolvency.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Recourse
cards.front: Recourse via NEGOTIORUM GESTIO: when is the guarantor's payment useful to the debtor?
cards.back:
Normally, since it frees the debtor — if the guarantor acts with ANIMUS RECIPIENDI, not to donate.
• Not useful: paying a non-existent debt or one with a permanent EXCEPTIO.
• Then CONDICTIO INDEBITI against the creditor (Ulpian D 12.6.25, Case 51 e).

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Recourse
cards.front: Surety against the principal debtor's express wish — does he have recourse?
cards.back:
Disputed: most refuse the ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA; some grant it or an ACTIO UTILIS.
• Against: Paulus and Pomponius D 17.1.40 (Case 223/1); Julian, followed by Justinian (Case 223/2).
• For: the debtor is freed at the guarantor's expense — enrichment.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Recourse
cards.front: BENEFICIUM CEDENDARUM ACTIONUM: how did recourse by assignment develop?
cards.back:
Classical agreed assignment → Justinian's right to demand it (CESSIO NECESSARIA) → modern CESSIO LEGIS (§ 1358 ABGB).
• Technique: MANDATUM IN REM SUAM — guarantor sues on the creditor's action.
• Advantage: pledges and other sureties attached to the claim pass too.
• Guarantor 'buys' the claim (Paulus D 46.1.36, Case 51 h).

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Co-suretyship
cards.front: LEX APULEIA vs LEX FURIA DE SPONSU — position of co-guarantors?
cards.back:
Both only for SPONSIO and FIDEPROMISSIO; APULEIA: joint liability plus internal recourse; FURIA: several liability.
• APULEIA: creditor claims all from one, who recovers shares from the others.
• FURIA: creditor must sue each for his share — higher litigation costs.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Co-suretyship
cards.front: Joint vs several liability?
cards.back: Joint: each debtor owes the whole (IN SOLIDUM), creditor receives it only once; several: each owes only a proportionate part.

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Co-suretyship
cards.front: EPISTULA HADRIANI — what does it give co-FIDEIUSSORES?
cards.back:
Proportionate liability of all solvent co-guarantors, who share the insolvency risk; plus the BENEFICIUM DIVISIONIS.
• Before: joint full liability (Gai Inst 3.121).
• Invoker must prove the others' solvency: EXCEPTIO SI NON ET ILLI SOLVENDI SINT.
• Paid all without invoking it → recourse only by assigned claim (Modestinus D 46.1.39, Case 51 d).

cards.topic: Ch. XIII — Suretyship: Co-suretyship
cards.front: Example 82: D owes C 120,000; W, X, Y, Z are sureties; D is insolvent. What can C take from W under LEX APULEIA, LEX FURIA, EPISTULA HADRIANI?
cards.back:
APULEIA: all 120,000 (W then recovers 30,000 from each); FURIA: 30,000; HADRIANI: 30,000.
• Under HADRIANI, if one co-surety is insolvent, the three solvent ones owe 40,000 each.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Property law and enrichment
cards.front: What is unjustified enrichment, and which remedies reverse it?
cards.back:
Assets moved without justifying legal cause to someone not entitled; reversed mainly by CONDICTIONES, also ACTIONES IN FACTUM.
• Ex 83: Agatha pays Belias a non-debt; he mixes the coins → CONDICTIO.
• Ex 84: Castor plants Pomona's olive trees, owner by accession → her ACTIO IN FACTUM.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Property law and enrichment
cards.front: Property link: REI VINDICATIO or CONDICTIO — how do you decide after a failed transfer?
cards.back:
Ask whether ownership passed: if not, the owner vindicates the thing; if yes, only an enrichment CONDICTIO.
• TRADITIO without IUSTA CAUSA → no ownership → REI VINDICATIO.
• Ownership passed (mixing, PRO SOLUTO, MANCIPATIO) → CONDICTIO in personam.
• REI VINDICATIO lies against any possessor; CONDICTIO only against the recipient.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Property law and enrichment
cards.front: Examples 85 and 86: a slave delivers Agrippa's statue to the wrong address; PRODIGUS Philto sells a vase without his curator. Remedy?
cards.back:
REI VINDICATIO: without IUSTA CAUSA no ownership passed.
• Ex 85: Cassandra has no cause either for acquiring or for keeping.
• Ex 86: curator's consent lacking → REI VINDICATIO (or ACTIO PUBLICIANA) against Helena.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Property law and enrichment
cards.front: When does a recipient become owner yet still owe restitution under the law of obligations?
cards.back:
Exceptionally: PRO SOLUTO without debt, abstract conveyance, later loss of cause, or original acquisition.
• Abstract MANCIPATIO / IN IURE CESSIO pass ownership even if the causa was void.
• Contract dissolved EX NUNC → recipient must re-transfer.
• Not after USUCAPIO: the usucapient owes nothing; nor the BONA FIDEI POSSESSOR for fruits.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Property law and enrichment
cards.front: Example 87: Cato promises Felix 100 by abstract stipulation, meant as DOS; the marriage fails; Felix sues. Defence?
cards.back:
The abstract promise is valid, but Cato has the EXCEPTIO DOLI; later also a CONDICTIO LIBERATIONIS.
• Shows: claims, too, can be acquired without justification.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Property law and enrichment
cards.front: What is a CONDICTIO, and is it only an enrichment action?
cards.back:
An ACTIO IN PERSONAM for a specific sum (CERTA PECUNIA) or specific thing (CERTA RES).
• Also contractual: loan repayment (ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE), stipulated CERTUM.
• Enrichment types: INDEBITI, OB REM, OB TURPEM CAUSAM.
• CONDICTIO EX CAUSA FURTIVA: from a modern view delictual.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Property law and enrichment
cards.front: What are the two meanings of CONDICTIO SINE CAUSA?
cards.back: Narrow: restitution after an abstract conveyance (MANCIPATIO, IN IURE CESSIO) without valid causa; broad: umbrella for all enrichment condictions.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: CONDICTIO INDEBITI
cards.front: What are the requirements of the CONDICTIO INDEBITI?
cards.back:
Performance (DATIO), not owed (INDEBITUM), made by mistake.
• Aim: reverse a transfer made to perform a supposed obligation.
• Gaius classes it as a real obligation (Gai Inst 3.91, Case 229).

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: CONDICTIO INDEBITI
cards.front: What counts as 'performance' for the CONDICTIO INDEBITI?
cards.back:
A DATIO making the recipient owner, intentionally given and intentionally received.
• Recipient not owner → REI VINDICATIO / ACTIO PUBLICIANA instead.
• Ex 88: Cara's iron soldered to a statue → accession, no performance; maybe ACTIO IN FACTUM.
• Building on another's land: no CONDICTIO, only retention (Julian D 12.6.33, Case 230).

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: CONDICTIO INDEBITI
cards.front: Which payments count as 'not owed' (INDEBITUM) — and which not?
cards.back:
Not owed: non-existent debt, permanent EXCEPTIO, unfulfilled condition, ward without tutor; owed: natural obligations, early payment.
• Ex 89: payment despite PACTUM DE NON PETENDO → reclaimable.
• Ward: Neratius D 12.6.41 (Case 232); condition: Pomponius D 12.6.16 pr.
• SC MACEDONIANUM repayment; early payment (Paulus D 12.6.10): no CONDICTIO.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: CONDICTIO INDEBITI
cards.front: CONDICTIO INDEBITI: what if the payer, or the recipient, knew there was no debt?
cards.back:
Payer knew: no CONDICTIO — he is SIMILIS EI QUI DONAT; recipient knew: FURTUM → ACTIO FURTI and CONDICTIO FURTIVA.
• Mistake of law probably suffices; § 1431 ABGB expressly.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: OB REM, OB TURPEM CAUSAM, FURTIVA
cards.front: CONDICTIO OB REM (CAUSA DATA CAUSA NON SECUTA) — when does it lie?
cards.back:
Performance given for an expected counter-performance or event, without enforceable contract — and the expectation fails.
• CAUSA DATA: the agreement suffices for ownership to pass.
• CAUSA NON SECUTA: only remedy is reclaiming one's own performance.
• Ex 90: Prosper gives 1,000 DOS; the marriage never happens.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: OB REM, OB TURPEM CAUSAM, FURTIVA
cards.front: CONDICTIO OB REM vs CONDICTIO OB CAUSAM FINITAM?
cards.back:
OB REM: counter-performance typically unenforceable; OB CAUSAM FINITAM: an originally enforceable cause later falls away.
• Launderer pays for lost clothes; owner finds them → contract action or CONDICTIO (Cassius in Ulpian D 12.7.2).

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: OB REM, OB TURPEM CAUSAM, FURTIVA
cards.front: CONDICTIO OB TURPEM VEL INIUSTAM CAUSAM — when does it lie, and when not?
cards.back:
Restitution of performance for an immoral or prohibited purpose, even if achieved — unless the payer is equally to blame.
• Ex 91 'your money or your life'; Ex 92 unagreed 'reward' to return jewellery.
• IN PARI TURPITUDINE MELIOR EST CAUSA POSSIDENTIS.
• Bribing the IUDEX: no restitution (Paulus D 12.5.3, Case 238).

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: OB REM, OB TURPEM CAUSAM, FURTIVA
cards.front: Property link: what does the CONDICTIO FURTIVA add to the owner's REI VINDICATIO against a thief?
cards.back:
Liability for the value even after the thing is gone: FUR SEMPER IN MORA EST.
• The thief never becomes owner; REI VINDICATIO needs the thing still existing.
• CONDICTIO FURTIVA lies only against the FUR (or a knowing receiver).
• Both reipersecutory → choose one; cumulate with the penal ACTIO FURTI.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Payment orders (DELEGATIO)
cards.front: Payment order (DELEGATIO): name the three persons and the three relationships.
cards.back:
Delegator A, delegatee B, obligee C.
• A–B: cover relationship; A–C: underlying debt relationship; B–C: performance relationship.
• Ex 93: B's payment to C discharges B's debt to A and A's debt to C at once.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Payment orders (DELEGATIO)
cards.front: Active vs passive delegation (DELEGATIO OBLIGANDI)?
cards.back:
Active: novation with change of creditor (C replaces A); passive: novation with change of debtor (B replaces A).
• Active: B keeps his defences against A (Ex 94: price reduction).
• Passive: B can raise A's defences against C (Ex 95: loan of 500).

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Payment orders (DELEGATIO)
cards.front: Unwinding a payment order: who sues whom if the cover, the underlying, or both relationships are defective?
cards.back:
Cover defective: B against A; underlying defective: A against C; both defective: B directly against C.
• The valid relationship stays unaffected.
• Ex 96: B pays C's DOS for A, owing A nothing → CONDICTIO INDEBITI against A.
• Ex 97: both defective → B's CONDICTIO against C (Julian D 12.4.7 pr, Case 234).

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Cessation of enrichment and praetorian remedies
cards.front: Must a CONDICTIO defendant pay if he is no longer enriched?
cards.back:
In principle yes — fixed by what was received; but a good-faith disposer is released, except for a surrogate.
• Knowing disposer: estimated value.
• Thing perished: liable if negligent or already in delay.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Cessation of enrichment and praetorian remedies
cards.front: Paulus D 12.6.65.8 (Case 229 a): E mistakenly delivers an unowed slave to T, who frees him. What does E's CONDICTIO aim at?
cards.back:
T in bad faith: the slave's value; T in good faith: only the OPERAE LIBERORUM and his inheritance right.
• This replacement asset = 'substitute commodum'.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Cessation of enrichment and praetorian remedies
cards.front: Which praetorian remedies balance shifts of assets not based on performance?
cards.back:
Retention for a BONA FIDE possessor's expenses; ACTIO IN FACTUM after ACCESSIO or SPECIFICATIO; ACTIO UTILIS after consumption.
• Ex 98: Thisbe builds on Eudemos' land (SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT).
• NEMINEM CUM ALTERIUS DETRIMENTO ET INIURIA FIERI LOCUPLETIOREM (Pomponius D 50.17.206).
• Amount: QUANTO LOCUPLETIOR FACTUS EST — claimant bears any excess loss.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Cessation of enrichment and praetorian remedies
cards.front: Pomponius D 46.3.66 (Case 231): ward A, without his tutor, orders B to pay A's creditor C; B wrongly thinks he owes A. B's claim?
cards.back:
No CONDICTIO INDEBITI against the ward, but an ACTIO UTILIS for QUANTO LOCUPLETIOR FACTUS EST.
• Ward enriched by the full sum: his real debt to C was discharged.
• CONDICTIO recovers the sum paid; ACTIO UTILIS only the present enrichment.

cards.topic: Ch. XIV — Unjustified enrichment: Cessation of enrichment and praetorian remedies
cards.front: Example 100: why is the ACTIO DE IN REM VERSO also an enrichment remedy?
cards.back:
The VERSIO is both ground and cap of the DOMINUS' liability.
• Slave borrows 1,000 for a summer house; land value rises 800.
• Mistress would have built anyway: 1,000 saved; otherwise: 800.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: Damages basics
cards.front: Who bears the loss from harm, and when does it shift to someone else?
cards.back:
Basic rule: the person whose goods are affected; it shifts to whoever caused the harm unlawfully and culpably.
• Ex 101: villa worth 800,000 struck by lightning — the owner's loss.
• Ex 103: neighbour Ares sets it on fire → damages claim of 800,000.
• Roman risk-sharing like insurance: SOCIETAS, FENUS NAUTICUM.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: Damages basics
cards.front: Damages EX CONTRACTU vs EX DELICTO?
cards.back:
EX CONTRACTU: breach of contractually assumed duties; EX DELICTO: breach of duties binding everyone, defined as delicts.
• Ex 105: Leonidas eats the sold bull; Burrus buys another for 1,200 → 200 contractual damages.
• Delict core: harm to absolutely protected property and bodily integrity.
• Ex 106: Lysippe's galloping horse injures senator Cato.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: Damages basics
cards.front: Indemnification (INDEMNITAS) vs penalty (POENA)?
cards.back:
INDEMNITAS makes good the loss and never exceeds it; POENA aims at punishment and deterrence.
• Roman private penalty goes to the injured party, on top of compensation.
• Modern continental law reserves punishment for the state.
• Anglo-American punitive damages, e.g. Rock Hudson case: $ 7,250,000 against assistant Miller.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: INIURIA and FURTUM
cards.front: What is the delict INIURIA, and what does it require?
cards.back:
Violation of personality rights — honour and physical integrity of free Romans; requires DOLUS (ANIMUS INIURIANDI).
• E.g. a mocking caterwauling 'concert'; deliberate bodily injury.
• ACTIO INIURIARUM: penal; victim's own estimate, reviewed AEQUUM ET BONUM.
• Injuring another's slave intentionally: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM and INIURIA to the DOMINUS.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: INIURIA and FURTUM
cards.front: What is FURTUM, and how broad is it?
cards.back:
Appropriating, without authority and intending to enrich oneself, a movable known to be another's.
• Only movables (Gai Inst 2.51).
• Includes embezzlement; FURTUM USUS = misusing a deposited or borrowed thing (Gai Inst 3.196).
• DOLUS must show in an outward act of taking control.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: INIURIA and FURTUM
cards.front: Who besides the owner can sue for FURTUM — and can the owner commit it?
cards.back:
Holders liable for CUSTODIA (e.g. pledgees, borrowers), if solvent; the owner can commit FURTUM himself.
• Owner taking his own thing from someone with a right of retention (Julian D 47.2.60(59), Case 30).

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: INIURIA and FURTUM
cards.front: Which remedies lie for FURTUM, and how do they combine?
cards.back:
Penal ACTIO FURTI plus one reipersecutory remedy — CONDICTIO FURTIVA or REI VINDICATIO.
• FURTUM MANIFESTUM: fourfold; NEC MANIFESTUM: double the value.
• Penal + reipersecutory: cumulation of actions.
• CONDICTIO FURTIVA vs REI VINDICATIO: elect one before the praetor.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, DOLUS, METUS
cards.front: What is DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, and which chapters of the LEX AQUILIA matter?
cards.back:
Delict of destroying or damaging property, built by the jurists on the LEX AQUILIA.
• Ch. 1: OCCIDERE of slaves and four-legged herd animals.
• Ch. 3: URERE, FRANGERE, RUMPERE — widened to CORRUMPERE.
• Killing a dog or goose → ch. 3; indirect harm → ACTIONES IN FACTUM / UTILES.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, DOLUS, METUS
cards.front: Why is the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE an ACTIO MIXTA?
cards.back:
It compensates lost value but also has a (minor) penal element.
• Ch. 1: highest value in the past year — may exceed the real loss.
• Several wrongdoers each liable in full (Ulpian D 9.2.11.2: CUM SIT POENA).
• Denial of the deed → double (Gai Inst 4.9).

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, DOLUS, METUS
cards.front: What is the delict DOLUS, and what is special about the ACTIO DE DOLO?
cards.back:
Harming someone by malicious deceit or bad-faith conduct; the ACTIO DE DOLO is reipersecutory and subsidiary.
• Compensation plus any gain the deceiver made.
• Not for BONA FIDES obligations (contracts, NEGOTIORUM GESTIO): good faith covers deceit.
• EXCEPTIO DOLI: also a right of retention against restitution claims.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, DOLUS, METUS
cards.front: METUS: which three remedies does classical law give?
cards.back:
RESTITUTIO IN INTEGRUM, ACTIO QUOD METUS CAUSA, EXCEPTIO METUS.
• Requires a serious, unlawful or immoral restriction of freedom.
• ACTIO: generally fourfold, avoided by restoring before judgment.
• Framed 'in rem': also against the coercer's good-faith successors.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: Concept of damage
cards.front: DAMNUM EMERGENS vs LUCRUM CESSANS?
cards.back:
DAMNUM EMERGENS: loss in value of existing assets; LUCRUM CESSANS: lost profit — only if realistic, not speculative.
• Differential method: market value before vs after the injury.
• Villa burnt: 800,000 DAMNUM EMERGENS.
• Lost serious offer of 950,000: 150,000 LUCRUM CESSANS.

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: Concept of damage
cards.front: Ulpian (Vivianus) D 9.2.27.28: a slave boy is castrated without permission and his value rises. Claim?
cards.back:
No DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM: the owner's assets are not diminished.
• If intentional: INIURIA to the DOMINUS → ACTIO INIURIARUM.
• Parallel: picking ripe fruit — no loss; unripe fruit — LEX AQUILIA (D 9.2.27.25).

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: Concept of damage
cards.front: Can a free Roman claim damages for bodily injury or pain?
cards.back:
No general rule: LIBERUM CORPUS NON RECIPIT AESTIMATIONEM (Gaius D 9.1.3) — only INIURIA and penal offences.
• Slaves: LEX AQUILIA, as the owner's material loss.
• Exception: shoemaker's apprentice (Case 276).
• Modern: pain and suffering (§ 1325 ABGB, § 847 BGB).

cards.topic: Ch. XV — Infliction of harm: Concept of damage
cards.front: Paulus (Pedius) D 9.2.33 pr (Case 278): A kills B's slave X, who is B's natural son. Is B's grief compensated?
cards.back:
No: Roman law disregards affection value — only the material loss counts.
• Emotional harm only via INIURIA with ANIMUS INIURIANDI (Ex 107: horse injured to insult its owner).
• Contrast § 1331 ABGB: affection value for wilful or malicious harm.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Text and assessment scheme
cards.front: Quote the 1st chapter of the LEX AQUILIA and state its content.
cards.back:
SI QUIS SERVUM SERVAMVE ALIENUM ALIENAMVE QUADRUPEDEMVE PECUDEM INIURIA OCCIDERIT, QUANTI ID IN EO ANNO PLURIMI FUIT, TANTUM AES DARE DOMINO DAMNAS ESTO.
• Wrongful killing of another's slave or four-legged herd animal.
• Owner gets the highest value in that year (Gaius D 9.2.2 pr).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Text and assessment scheme
cards.front: Quote the 3rd chapter of the LEX AQUILIA and state its content.
cards.back:
SI QUIS ALTERI DAMNUM FAXIT, QUOD USSERIT FREGERIT RUPERIT INIURIA, QUANTI EA RES ERIT IN DIEBUS TRIGINTA PROXIMIS, TANTUM AES DOMINO DARE DAMNAS ESTO.
• Loss by wrongful burning, breaking or 'rending'.
• Owner gets what the matter comes to within the next 30 days (Ulpian D 9.2.27.5).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Text and assessment scheme
cards.front: When was the LEX AQUILIA passed, and why is the jurists' INTERPRETATIO so important?
cards.back:
Date uncertain, probably 3rd century BC; classical law rests on INTERPRETATIO, itself a source of law.
• Classical picture differed much from the wording some 300 years older.
• It repealed earlier statutes, e.g. Twelve Tables on OS FRACTUM (Ulpian D 9.2.1 pr).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Text and assessment scheme
cards.front: What are the four stages for assessing liability under the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.back:
1. Statutory definition (incl. causation); 2. unlawfulness (INIURIA, objective); 3. culpability (INIURIA, subjective); 4. amount.
• Stage 2: definition indicates unlawfulness, unless a justification applies.
• Stage 3: DOLUS or CULPA; check lawful excuses.
• Still the basic test for delictual (and contractual) liability.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Text and assessment scheme
cards.front: ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (DIRECTA) vs ACTIO IN FACTUM / UTILIS — why the graded concept?
cards.back:
Active, direct harm: injurer's role obvious → statute; indirect harm or omission: attribution less obvious → analogous actions.
• Also called ACTIO AD EXEMPLUM LEGIS AQUILIAE.
• A typology develops where the analogy is regularly granted.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Which animals are QUADRUPEDES PECUDES under ch. 1 (Gaius D 9.2.2.2)?
cards.back:
Herd animals: sheep, goats, cattle, mules, donkeys, working elephants and camels; pigs disputed (Labeo: yes).
• Not: dogs and wild animals (bears, lions, panthers) → ch. 3.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: What is OCCIDERE in the sense of ch. 1?
cards.back:
Active, immediate killing by direct physical action: SI QUIS CORPORE SUO DAMNUM DEDERIT (Gai Inst 3.219).
• Bare hands, heel, head, sword, cudgel, projectile (Ulpian D 9.2.7.1, Case 263).
• Load thrown down, botched operation, poison given to drink.
• VIS is usual but not required.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: What is MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE, and which remedy follows?
cards.back:
Providing a cause of death without direct action — by omission or indirect conduct; ACTIO UTILIS or IN FACTUM.
• Starving a slave one must feed (Ulpian (Neratius) D 9.2.9.2).
• Taking his clothes so he freezes (D 19.5.14.1); making his horse shy.
• Luring into a trap where B kills: A IN FACTUM, B LEGIS AQUILIAE (D 9.2.9.3).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Midwife's case, Ulpian (Labeo) D 9.2.9 pr (Case 264): a midwife gives a slave woman medicine and she dies. Liability?
cards.back:
Put into her mouth with the midwife's own hands → OCCIDERE → ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE.
• Merely handed over, the slave took it herself → MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE → ACTIO IN FACTUM.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Ulpian (Celsus) D 9.2.7.6 (Case 263): poison given instead of medicine; a sword handed to a mentally ill slave. Remedy?
cards.back:
ACTIO IN FACTUM for MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE: the slave acts by his own hand.
• Sword: suicide likely meant; killing another slave → IN FACTUM too.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Bridge case, Ulpian (Celsus) D 9.2.7.7 (Case 263): G pushes slave H off a bridge and he dies — from the push, sinking, or drowning later. Remedy? And a slave boy hurled against a rock?
cards.back:
ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE in every variant: G set the chain in motion — CORPORE SUO DAMNUM DEDIT.
• Whether death is immediate or later does not matter.
• Rock: death from impact, but direct physical contact → ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Ulpian (Proculus) D 9.2.7.3: N pushes O, who falls against slave P so that P dies. Who is liable?
cards.back:
N: no contact with P → ACTIO IN FACTUM; O: not liable, QUIA DAMNUM NON DEDERIT.
• Open whether O fails definition, unlawfulness or fault.
• Modern: O cannot be held responsible at all.
• Cf Neratius D 9.2.53: driving oxen onto a ridge → ACTIO IN FACTUM.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Dog case, Ulpian (Proculus, Julian) D 9.2.11.5: T provokes a dog, which bites slave U. Proculus vs Julian?
cards.back:
Proculus: ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE without distinction; Julian: only if T held the dog, otherwise ACTIO IN FACTUM.
• Held dog = T's direct instrument.
• Proculus perhaps: setting a dog on is like throwing a spear.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: What is URERE, and which examples give the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE?
cards.back:
Ch. 3: actively and directly singeing or setting on fire.
• Torch in a slave's face (D 9.2.27.6); firing a field or house (D 9.2.27.7).
• Neighbouring house catches fire → liable for each house (D 9.2.27.8).
• Killing a ch. 1 object by fire = OCCIDERE.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Ulpian (Celsus) Coll 12.7.4–5 (Case 265): A burns straw on his own field; the fire spreads to B's field. Remedy?
cards.back:
Majority: ACTIO IN FACTUM — burning straw is no typical cause of fire on a neighbour's field; minority: ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE.
• Contrast: Roman tenements typically spread fire → ACTIO DIRECTA for each house.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Oven attendant's case, Ulpian (Neratius) D 9.2.27.9: tenant C's slave E carelessly watches (or sleeps by) a fire; the rented villa burns. Liability?
cards.back:
Careful stoker F: not liable (NON PECCAVIT); E: omission → ACTIO UTILIS, falling asleep is NEGLEGENTIA.
• Tenant C: ACTIO EX LOCATO for CULPA IN ELIGENDO.
• Landlord D must choose contract or delict.
• Delict: C noxally liable — pay or surrender E (NOXAE DEDITIO).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: FRANGERE and RUMPERE — what do they cover?
cards.back:
FRANGERE = breaking; RUMPERE = originally an open wound or bruise, later any injury, also to inanimate objects.
• FRANGERE: glass cup (D 9.2.27.29, Case 273), door, building, bone.
• RUMPERE: overloaded mule, miscarriage by push, cut or soiled clothes, grain into river.
• CORRUMPERE: spilt or soured wine, grain mixed with sand.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: What is CORRUMPERE, and why did the broad reading of RUMPERE matter?
cards.back:
Umbrella term: any damage to property outside ch. 1 — even URERE and FRANGERE fit under it.
• Celsus in Ulpian D 9.2.27.16: a general term after specific ones is nothing new.
• Barrel drilled, wine leaks: direct → LEGIS AQUILIAE, or IN FACTUM (Labeo D 9.2.27.35).
• Rammed ship (D 9.2.29.2): ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE without labelling the act.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Depriving someone of property without damaging its substance — which remedy?
cards.back:
Not (COR)RUMPERE: with intent to enrich → FURTUM; otherwise an ACTIO IN FACTUM modelled on the LEX AQUILIA.
• Ring dropped into the Tiber (Alfenus D 19.5.23, Case 268); cup thrown into the sea.
• Cattle scared off with a red cloth, ending with thieves (D 47.2.50.4).
• Still requires unlawful and culpable conduct.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Proculus D 41.1.55: an 'animal lover' frees a boar from a hunter's trap. Remedy for the hunter?
cards.back:
ACTIO IN FACTUM: no ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (substance unharmed), no FURTUM (no intent to enrich).
• The hunter had already acquired possession and ownership.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Property link: why does the hunter in D 41.1.55 lose his property when the boar escapes?
cards.back:
A wild animal is owned only while held: once it regains natural freedom it is ownerless again.
• Hunter became owner by OCCUPATIO once it came into his power.
• So the loss is real though the boar is unharmed → ACTIO IN FACTUM.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Ulpian (Sabinus) D 9.2.27.21 (Case 267): A knocks coins out of B's hand. Liability?
cards.back:
Aim that a third party gets them → FURTUM; coins irretrievably lost (river, sea, sewer) → LEX AQUILIA or ACTIO IN FACTUM.
• Sabinus: irreversible loss equals destruction.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Paulus D 9.2.30.2 (Case 269): someone consumes another's wine or grain without permission. Remedy?
cards.back:
ACTIO UTILIS: consumption destroys the substance but uses it as intended, so ch. 3 not directly.
• No FURTUM if he mistook them for his own without DOLUS.
• Cattle eating neighbour's fallen acorns → ACTIO IN FACTUM (D 19.5.14.3).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: CONDICIO SINE QUA NON vs adequate causation?
cards.back:
Equivalence: every indispensable condition counts equally; adequacy: only conduct typically leading to such harm.
• Test: think the act away (omission: add correct conduct) — does the harm vanish?
• Ex 108: New Year firecracker singes B's coat (adequate), drives C to suicide (not).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Why do the Roman jurists not distinguish equivalent and adequate causation explicitly?
cards.back:
The typified acts (OCCIDERE, URERE, FRANGERE, RUMPERE) already imply causation and adequacy; it matters in analogous cases.
• Labeo (D 9.2.7.5): lightly pushing a sickly slave who dies → liable.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Paulus D 9.2.30.4: A gives B's slave a non-fatal wound; the slave dies because B neglects treatment. Liability?
cards.back:
Only VULNERARE (= RUMPERE, ch. 3), not OCCIDERE: the wound is causal but not the adequate cause of death.
• A does not answer for B's neglect.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Statutory definition and causation
cards.front: Overtaking, alternative and cumulative causation — Roman solutions?
cards.back:
Each injurer is liable in full.
• Overtaking: A's mortal wound, B's later beating kills — both liable (A: OCCIDERE or VULNERARE).
• Alternative: unclear who caused it — each as sole cause (Julian D 9.2.51.1).
• Cumulative: each act alone sufficient — each liable (Ulpian D 9.2.11.4).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: How is unlawfulness established under the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.back:
Meeting the statutory definition indicates unlawfulness (INIURIA OCCIDERE), unless a justification applies — then no liability; fault is not examined.
• Modern grounds: self-defence, necessity, permitted self-help, legal authorisation, consent.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: What are the requirements of self-defence as a justification?
cards.back:
Repelling a present, unlawful attack on protectable interests, proportionately and with no more harm than necessary.
• Not against lawful acts or self-defence; attacker need not be at fault.
• Harm to third parties not justified (Paulus D 9.2.45.4).
• Gaius D 9.2.4 pr (Case 270): killing a slave robber in ambush → not liable.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Lantern case, Alfenus D 9.2.52.1 (Case 271): P carries off innkeeper K's lantern; K pursues him and knocks out P's eye. Is K liable?
cards.back:
Not if P struck at him with a lance (self-defence); liable if he blinds an overpowered P, or starts the beating himself.
• Variant 2: counter-attack, intentional = excessive force.
• Variant 3: only cheap property attacked → disproportionate; negligent → liable.
• Killing the thief is not even considered.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Defence of others vs putative self-defence?
cards.back: Defence of others justifies like self-defence; putative self-defence (attack wrongly assumed) never justifies, but may exclude fault.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: When could a thief (FUR) be killed lawfully?
cards.back:
Twelve Tables: a thief defending himself with weapons, or caught at night; doubtful in classical law (Ulpian (Pomponius) Coll 7.3.2).
• Probably exceeds the developed concept of defending property.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: What are the requirements of necessity as a justification?
cards.back:
Harming a third party to save one's interests from imminent danger (not an unlawful attack): danger not self-caused, last resort, suitable.
• Weighing of goods matters more than in self-defence.
• Attacking animal → necessity, not self-defence.
• Saving another's interest is treated like necessity.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Ulpian (Labeo, Proculus) D 9.2.29.3 (Case 272): a storm drives A's ship into B's anchor lines and C's nets; the crew cuts them. Liable?
cards.back:
Blameless crew: justified by necessity. Crew (partly) to blame for entanglement: no justification, liable if culpable.
• Then only the nets' value, not the lost catch — speculative LUCRUM CESSANS.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Ulpian (Celsus) D 9.2.49.1: D tears down E's house to stop an approaching fire that never reaches it. Celsus vs Servius?
cards.back:
Celsus: justified if D acted IUSTO METU (objective, BONUS PATER FAMILIAS); Servius: not justified, liable if at fault.
• Clear case if the fire reaches E's site anyway.
• Servius' exception: magistrates pulling down houses (D 43.24.7.4).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Permitted self-help: unpermitted water pipe (Ulpian D 9.2.29.1) vs overhanging canopy (Proculus) — why different?
cards.back:
Removing the pipe through one's house: justified self-help. Tearing down the canopy: liable — he should have sued for removal.
• Pipe: rescript of Emperor Alexander Severus.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Property link: how far may an owner defend his property by self-help?
cards.back:
Only narrowly: VIM VI REPELLERE LICET against forcible dispossession; otherwise he must go to court.
• Retaking land seized by force (VI) is allowed.
• Pipe removed: justified; canopy torn down: liable (Proculus).
• Blinding a thief over a cheap lantern: excessive force.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Pomponius (Quintus Mucius) D 9.2.39 pr–1: F drives E's pregnant mare off his pasture and she miscarries. Q. Mucius vs Pomponius?
cards.back: Q. Mucius: F liable only if he beat or chased her too vigorously or maliciously; Pomponius: no justification, liable for all harm.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Unlawfulness and justification
cards.front: Special authorisation by the legal system and consent of the injured party — examples?
cards.back:
Magistrates may seize assets, smash beds on public roads, pull down houses: IURIS EXECUTIO NON HABET INIURIAM.
• Exceeding authority: liable, e.g. damaged seized goods (D 9.2.29.7).
• Consent: glass cutters' exclusion of accidental FRANGERE (D 9.2.27.29).
• Master entering slave in a contest; surgery covered only LEGE ARTIS.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: DOLUS vs CULPA — and what is the double meaning of CULPA?
cards.back:
DOLUS: harm foreseen and accepted (DIRECTUS or EVENTUALIS); CULPA: no intent, but due care (DILIGENTIA) neglected.
• CULPA broad = fault in general; narrow = negligence.
• Sources: NEGLEGENTIA, IMPERITIA, INFIRMITAS.
• CULPA LEVISSIMA suffices (Ulpian D 9.2.44 pr).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: Is the Aquilian standard of care subjective or objective?
cards.back:
Objective (CULPA IN ABSTRACTO): measured against the VIR BONUS / BONUS PATER FAMILIAS, varied by activity and role.
• BONUS MEDICUS, good muleteer, BONUS TONSOR.
• Due care observed → no liability, even if harm follows.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: Tree pruner's case, Paulus (Quintus Mucius) D 9.2.31 (Case 274): a pruner drops a branch that kills a passing slave. Liable?
cards.back:
Q. Mucius: CULPA if a path runs beneath and no timely warning was shouted. Paulus: no path → unforeseeable, not liable.
• Saw someone below and dropped anyway → DOLUS, liable.
• Victim's own carelessness not discussed.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: Alfenus D 9.2.52.4: in a ball game a player pushes a slave boy, who falls and breaks a leg. Liable?
cards.back:
No: CASUS, not fault — even a careful player need not play so as never to injure.
• FRANGERE fulfilled, unlawful; liability fails at fault.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: Which circumstances preclude fault?
cards.back:
Mental incapacity, and acting on the command of a DOMINUS, PATER FAMILIAS or principal.
• No capacity: FURIOSUS, INFANS (to 7); IMPUBERES INFANTIA MAIORES judged individually (D 9.2.5.2).
• The act stays unlawful → self-defence against it possible.
• On command: ACTIO DIRECTA against the power-holder (D 9.2.44.1).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: Culpa compensation vs acting at one's own risk?
cards.back:
Both free the injurer entirely — Roman law does not split losses; one offsets fault against carelessness, the other removes the duty of care.
• Culpa compensation: never offsets the injurer's DOLUS.
• Own risk: voluntary entry into danger — sports, trespassing.
• Modern law divides the loss (§ 1304 ABGB).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: Barber's case, Ulpian (Mela, Proculus) D 9.2.11 pr: a hard-thrown ball hits a barber's hand and the razor cuts the slave's throat. Who is liable?
cards.back:
Proculus: shaving where balls fly is negligent, yet whoever entrusts himself to a barber in a dangerous spot has himself to blame.
• A BONUS TONSOR must shield clients.
• Mela: whoever was at fault is liable — possibly the ball player.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Fault
cards.front: Javelin thrower's case, Ulpian D 9.2.9.4: when is a javelin thrower liable for killing a slave?
cards.back:
Throwing for fun: CULPA, liable; on a practice field: not liable; aiming deliberately at a crossing slave: DOLUS, liable.
• Practice-field explanations: own risk, culpa compensation, or no CULPA at all.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: Amount under ch. 1 vs ch. 3 of the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.back:
Ch. 1: highest value in the year before; ch. 3: what the matter comes to within the next 30 days.
• Year counted from death (Celsus) or mortal injury (Julian, prevailing).
• PLURIMI read into ch. 3 by interpretation (Ulpian D 9.2.29.8).
• 30 days: watch healing, include lasting damage.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: What does compensation of the 'interest' include in Aquilian case law?
cards.back:
Position as if no harm (difference method): DAMNUM EMERGENS plus probable LUCRUM CESSANS, calculated individually.
• Group loss: troupe slave, quadriga horse (Paulus D 9.2.22.1, Case 277).
• Inheritance the slave would have acquired; medical costs.
• Not: affection value (Case 278).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: Shoemaker's apprentice, Ulpian (Julian) D 9.2.5.3–9.2.7 pr (Case 276): a free son in power is injured. Can his father sue?
cards.back:
Yes, for medical costs and lost income — presumably an ACTIO UTILIS modelled on ch. 3.
• A son in power resembles a slave.
• The poor father depends on his earnings — financial loss.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE concurring with a contract action or REI VINDICATIO — choose or cumulate?
cards.back:
In principle choose (both reipersecutory); Paulus D 44.7.34.2: after ACTIO COMMODATI, Aquilian claim for the excess.
• Same after CONDICTIO FURTIVA (D 47.1.2.3).
• Compensated via REI VINDICATIO → Aquilian action given up (D 6.1.13).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: Theft followed by destruction, or a ch. 3 injury followed by death — which actions lie?
cards.back:
Stealing then killing a slave (D 9.2.27 pr) or destroying documents: ACTIO FURTI and ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE.
• Paulus D 47.2.28: documents → only FURTUM.
• Taking merely to destroy: only LEX AQUILIA (D 9.2.41.1).
• Ch. 3 then death: ch. 1 too, capped by EXCEPTIO DOLI (Julian D 9.2.47).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: Property link: who besides the owner can sue under the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.back:
Primarily the owner (D 9.2.11.6); by analogous action also usufructuary, usuary, pledgee and BONA FIDE possessor — even against the owner.
• USUSFRUCTUS: right to use and take fruits of another's thing, substance preserved.
• Pledgee: up to his secured claim; Paulus only if no other satisfaction.
• Co-owners: by share (D 9.2.19, 20).

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: Lessee or borrower with CUSTODIA duty — analogous Aquilian action against a third party?
cards.back:
Disputed: yes if CUSTODIA makes him answer for DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM (possibly Marcellus); Julian: no, he is not liable.
• Julian D 13.6.19 (Case 27); Ulpian D 19.2.41, D 9.2.11.9.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: Active and passive heritability of the Aquilian claim?
cards.back:
Actively heritable; passively not — liability ends with the perpetrator's death, except his enrichment (Ulpian D 9.2.23.8).
• Between death and entry: claim of the HEREDITAS IACENS.
• Noxal liability ends if the slave dies or is freed.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: What is litiscrescence under the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.back: A defendant who denies liability before the praetor and is then found liable pays double (DUPLUM) — Gai Inst 4.9.

cards.topic: Ch. XVI — Lex Aquilia: Amount, concurrence, parties
cards.front: Noxal liability: how does it work, and when is NOXAE DEDITIO excluded?
cards.back:
Check the dependant's own liability, then sue the current power-holder (NOXA CAPUT SEQUITUR): he pays or surrenders him (NOXAE DEDITIO).
• Surrender pays off when damages exceed the slave's value.
• Excluded if the principal knew and could prevent it, or ordered it → ACTIO DIRECTA.
• Ulpian (Celsus) D 9.4.2 pr; Paulus D 9.2.45 pr.
